item.title: Iranian cluster missiles hit Haifa area as war nears sixth week
item.description:
Iran launched ballistic missiles armed with cluster munitions at northern Israel on Friday morning, striking multiple sites in the Haifa area and wounding at least one person as the U.S.-Israel war against Iran entered its 35th day with no signs of abating.

A 79-year-old man was lightly wounded by cluster munition debris after an Iranian ballistic missile struck a home in Kiryat Ata, near Haifa, according to the Times of Israel and the Jerusalem Post. Emergency services responded to at least 10 impact sites across Haifa and surrounding towns, where damage was reported to roads and vehicles. The IDF assessed that the Iranian missiles were equipped with cluster munition warheads, which scatter explosive submunitions over wide areas.

item.title: Investors tune out Trump as Iran war roils energy markets
item.description: More than a month after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for joint U.S.-Israeli military strikes, the global fallout from the conflict is rippling far beyond oil prices — threatening critical helium supplies, rattling semiconductor manufacturers, and accelerating the world's pivot toward renewable energy.

item.title: Doctors Without Borders confirms Gaza supply shutdown since January
item.description:
Doctors Without Borders warned this week that Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza have pushed healthcare services to a breaking point, with the organization unable to bring any medical supplies into the territory since January 1.

In a testimony published on the MSF website on April 3, Dr. Randa Abu El-Khair Masoud, the organization's project medical referent in Gaza, said nearly 50 percent of essential chronic medications are critically low, including treatments for diabetes, hypertension, thyroid conditions, and respiratory diseases. MSF has already stopped accepting new patients for its non-communicable disease services, limiting care to existing patients.

"The needs in Gaza are massive, yet not enough aid is entering because Israeli authorities are blocking it. Just outside of Gaza, there are trucks with food and medicine waiting, yet they are blocked," Masoud said.

item.title: French, Japanese ships cross Hormuz in first Western transits since Iran war
item.description: A French-owned container ship and a Japanese-linked LNG tanker crossed the Strait of Hormuz this week, marking the first transits by Western European and Japanese vessels since Iran imposed a near-total blockade of the waterway following U.S.-Israeli strikes on February 28.

item.title: Satellite images confirm Iran damaged $136M US radar in Saudi Arabia
item.description: New satellite imagery has confirmed that an Iranian strike on March 1 damaged a U.S. AN/TPY-2 radar system at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, according to CNN reporting published this week. The radar is a core component of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile interception system, one of the most advanced missile-tracking platforms in the American arsenal.

item.title: German FM warns Trump's NATO exit threat risks alliance
item.description: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has publicly expressed alarm over President Donald Trump's latest threat to pull the United States out of NATO, calling the alliance of "enormous importance" to Germany and all its members as a widening transatlantic rift over the Iran conflict rattles European capitals.

item.title: U.S. tells Israel Iran negotiations have hit a deadlock
item.description: Five weeks into the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the conflict's cascading economic and humanitarian toll is reshaping energy markets, stranding thousands of mariners, and frustrating diplomatic efforts to bring fighting to an end. On Friday, the U.S. informed Israel that negotiations with Iran had hit a deadlock, even as tentative signs of resumed commercial shipping offered a sliver of hope in the otherwise shuttered Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Gaza Christians mark Good Friday as ceasefire strains
item.description:
Gaza City’s Christian community gathered at the Holy Family Church on Friday to mark Good Friday, a subdued observance that came as the enclave’s ceasefire with Israel remained in place but under strain. The service followed Palm Sunday celebrations at the same church less than a week earlier, one of the clearest signs that Holy Week rites have resumed in Gaza after long disruption from war.

The prayers unfolded against a backdrop of continuing insecurity. Reuters reported on March 31 that Gaza health officials said Israeli fire had killed at least 700 people since the ceasefire took hold, while the Associated Press has described the truce as tenuous and marked by near-daily violence. That has left Gaza’s remaining Christians celebrating Easter season with caution rather than relief.

item.title: Iran drone strike on Riyadh embassy far worse than disclosed
item.description: The March 3 Iranian drone strike on the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, caused far more destruction than the American and Saudi governments publicly acknowledged, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing current and former U.S. officials. Multiple floors of the embassy were heavily damaged, parts of the building remain "unrecoverable," and a fire sparked by the attack burned for twelve hours — a stark contrast to the Saudi Defense Ministry's initial assessment of "limited fire and minor material damage".

item.title: U.S. jet shot down over Iran as bridge strike death toll rises to 13
item.description:
A U.S. airstrike on Thursday destroyed the B1 bridge in Iran's Alborz province, a 136-meter structure that was the tallest bridge in the Middle East, killing at least eight people and wounding 95 others, according to Iranian officials. The death toll later climbed to 13 by Friday, Iranian state media reported.

The strike marks a sharp escalation in the targeting of Iranian civilian infrastructure as Operation Epic Fury, which began on February 28, enters its fifth week.

item.title: Italy extends fuel tax cut as Iran war strains global economies
item.description: Just over a month into the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, the economic fallout is rippling far beyond the Middle East, battering energy-dependent economies in Asia and straining European fiscal frameworks. South Korea and Japan, both heavily reliant on Persian Gulf energy imports, have emerged as the non-combatant nations bearing the heaviest burden, while European governments scramble to shield households from surging fuel costs.

item.title: Iran refuses ceasefire talks as U.S. jet downed over Iran
item.description: Diplomatic efforts to end the five-week-old war between the United States and Iran unraveled on Friday as Tehran formally refused to participate in talks proposed for Islamabad, and Qatar confirmed it would not serve as lead mediator — leaving regional powers scrambling to find a new path to negotiations even as the conflict escalated with the first downing of a U.S. combat aircraft over Iranian territory.

item.title: North Korea razes villages near key missile launch site
item.description: North Korea has demolished two villages near its main satellite and missile launch facility and tested an upgraded solid-fuel rocket engine, developments that analysts say point to an accelerating weapons buildup as the United States remains consumed by its military campaign in the Middle East.

item.title: Pakistan faces LNG crisis as Iran war chokes Asian economies
item.description: Five weeks into the conflict triggered by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is sending economic shockwaves far beyond the Middle East, with Asian economies bearing the brunt of what the International Energy Agency has called the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market."

item.title: U.S. Embassy urges Americans to leave Lebanon over Iran university threats
item.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued an urgent security alert on Friday urging all American citizens to depart Lebanon while commercial flights remain available, warning that Iran and its allied militias "may intend to target universities in Lebanon."

The advisory described the security environment as "volatile and unpredictable," citing ongoing airstrikes, drone activity, and rocket fire across the country, particularly in southern Lebanon, the Beqaa region, and parts of Beirut. "Iran has specifically threatened American universities across the Middle East," the embassy said, though it did not identify any specific institutions at risk.

item.title: Min Aung Hlaing wins parliamentary vote to become Myanmar president
item.description:
Myanmar's former military chief Min Aung Hlaing was elected president on Friday by the country's junta-installed parliament, completing a transition five years in the making from coup leader to nominal civilian head of state. The 69-year-old general, who seized power in 2021 by ousting the democratically elected government of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, won the presidency in a bicameral vote that was widely seen as a foregone conclusion, with pro-military lawmakers controlling roughly 86 percent of parliamentary seats.

The vote, held at 10:00 a.m. local time in the capital Naypyidaw, saw members of both legislative chambers choose from among three vice-presidential candidates: Min Aung Hlaing, Nan Ni Ni Aye of the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party, and former Prime Minister U Nyo Saw, a retired lieutenant general and close Min Aung Hlaing ally. Union Parliament Speaker U Aung Lin Dwe had confirmed on Thursday that all three candidates met the constitutional qualifications for the presidency.

item.title: Asia fuel crisis deepens as Songkran, Easter travel face sweeping flight cuts
item.description: A cascading jet fuel crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israel military strikes on Iran on February 28 is upending travel plans across two continents as the Easter holiday weekend and Southeast Asia's Songkran New Year celebrations approach, with airlines slashing routes, raising fares, and warning of further disruptions ahead.

item.title: Debris from intercepted drones hits buildings across Dubai
item.description: Debris from an intercepted Iranian drone struck the facade of Oracle's building in Dubai Internet City early Saturday, as the Gulf conflict entered its fifth week with no sign of abating. The Dubai Media Office confirmed the incident in a post on X, calling it a "minor incident" and saying no injuries were reported.

item.title: Iran's Khamenei has 'no role in leadership' due to severe injuries, report says
item.description:
More than a month after Israeli fighter jets struck the supreme leader's compound in Tehran, Iran's new leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public, and a hospital source has told The Media Line that he remains in a medical intensive care unit at an underground location with devastating injuries including a nonfunctional arm, paralyzed leg, spinal cord damage, and brain trauma.

The detailed account, published by The Media Line on Thursday, represents the most comprehensive report yet on the 56-year-old cleric's condition since the February 28 strike that killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with Mojtaba's wife, son, and several senior military officials.

item.title: Artemis II crew now closer to moon than Earth
item.description:
NASA on Friday unveiled the first photographs taken by the Artemis II crew, showing Earth in vivid detail as the four astronauts voyage toward the moon on the first crewed lunar mission in more than 50 years.

The images, captured by mission commander Reid Wiseman through a window of the Orion spacecraft, show Earth's blue oceans draped in swirling white clouds, with green auroras shimmering at the poles. One photograph, titled "Hello, World," depicts the Atlantic Ocean bordered by a thin halo of atmosphere as Earth casts a shadow on the sun. Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen said the crew was "glued to the window" as they watched their home planet shrink behind them.
